sections.heading: What the model learns from text
Preparing the text is the project

slides.title: Continued *pretraining*
slides.text: How does a model learn your field from the text you already hold?

narration: This chapter is about teaching a model your field of work.
It learns from text your organisation already holds.
Think of contracts, support tickets and manuals.

slides.caption: Continued pretraining teaches a model your field from text you already hold. Nobody has to write examples by hand.

slides.title: What we will *cover*
items: How a model learns from text
What changes once it is done

narration: This chapter is one of five ways to change the model itself.
You pick it when a model does not understand the language of your field.
First, we see how a model learns from text.
Then we compare that with training on written examples.
Next, we look at getting the text ready.
Then we see how to share out the training effort.
Last, we see what changes once the work is done.

slides.caption: This chapter covers how a model learns from text and how that differs from written examples. It then covers preparing the text, sharing the training, and what changes.

slides.title: The text is its own *teacher*
slides.picture: A line of text with the last word covered, and a model guessing the hidden word.

narration: First, how does a model learn from text at all?
It is shown some text with the next word hidden.
It guesses the hidden word.
Then it checks the real one.
It does this again and again, over huge amounts of text.
This is called pretraining.
Every next word is a small test with a known answer.
So nobody has to write the answers by hand.

slides.caption: A model learns by guessing each next word and checking the real one. This is called pretraining. The text holds every answer.

slides.title: The same training, *continued* on your text
slides.text: An existing model keeps learning from your own text.
slides.picture: A model that already read a large stack of general papers, now taking in a new stack of your own papers.

narration: Most models you use have already learned this way.
They learned from text on every kind of subject.
Now take one of those models.
Keep training it the same way, on your own text.
This is called continued pretraining.
The model keeps guessing next words.
But now the words come from your field.
It comes out reading your field the way your people do.

slides.caption: Continued pretraining keeps training an existing model the same way, on your own text. It learns to read your field the way your people do.

slides.title: Good guesses need *understanding*
slides.text: Guessing the next word well needs knowledge of the field.

narration: Why does guessing words teach the model anything?
To guess the next word well, the model must know what the words mean.
It must also know what tends to come next in that kind of document.
The model does this over billions of small pieces of text.
That forces it to learn the ideas of your field and how people write about them.

slides.caption: Guessing well needs knowledge of the field. Over billions of pieces of text, the model learns its ideas and its ways of writing.

slides.title: Models read *pieces* of words
slides.text: These small pieces are called tokens.
slides.picture: A long thread of small beads running into a model, one bead at a time.

narration: There is also a simple reason models misread specialist text.
It comes from how a model reads.
A model does not read whole words.
It reads text in small pieces.
A piece is often just part of a word.
These pieces are called tokens.
The rules for cutting text into tokens were learned from everyday text.

slides.caption: A model reads text in small pieces called tokens. The rules for cutting text into tokens come from everyday text.

slides.title: Specialist words get *broken up*
slides.picture: One long specialist word cut into several small broken pieces.

narration: Now take a word that only your field uses.
The cutting rules have rarely seen it.
So the word gets cut into four or five pieces that mean nothing.
The model has to put the word back together before it can use it.
Continued pretraining teaches the model how these words behave.
It learns to read them well in their cut-up form.

slides.caption: Cutting rules learned from everyday text break a specialist word into meaningless pieces. Continued pretraining teaches the model to read those words anyway.

slides.title: Often *confused* with fine-tuning
slides.text: Fine-tuning trains a model on examples people write by hand.

narration: So far, we have seen how the model learns from text.
People often confuse this with another kind of training.
In that kind, people write examples by hand.
Each example is a question and the answer they want.
This is called fine-tuning.
Both kinds train the model further.
But they do very different jobs.

slides.caption: Fine-tuning trains a model on questions and answers that people write by hand. It is often confused with continued pretraining.

slides.title: Two kinds of training, two *jobs*

narration: Here they are side by side.
Fine-tuning learns from thousands of written question and answer pairs.
Continued pretraining learns from text just as it already exists.
Text used just as it exists is called raw text.
It needs billions of tokens of it.
Fine-tuning teaches the model how to behave.
Someone has to write every answer.
Continued pretraining teaches the model what your field is.
Nobody writes anything.
But the text must be prepared first.

slides.caption: Fine-tuning uses thousands of written pairs to teach behaviour. Continued pretraining uses billions of tokens of raw text to teach the field.

slides.title: All the text together is the *corpus*
slides.text: Preparing it is where the project is won or lost.
slides.picture: Loose papers and folders gathered into one large box, with a model waiting beside it.

narration: We said the text must be prepared first.
Here is what that involves.
You gather all the text you plan to train on.
That whole collection is called the corpus.
The model takes in everything in the corpus.
It does not choose.
So preparing the corpus is where the project is won or lost.

slides.caption: All the text gathered for training is called the corpus. The model takes in all of it. Preparing it decides the project.

slides.title: Take out repeats and *noise*
slides.picture: A sieve over a stack of papers, with copies and torn pages set aside.

narration: Start by taking out repeats.
Old archives hold many templates and near-identical copies.
Whatever repeats gets too much weight in training.
Then filter out noise.
Failed scans, broken files and machine-made logs teach the model noise.

slides.caption: Remove repeats. Templates and copies should not get too much weight. Filter out failed scans, broken files and machine-made logs.

slides.title: Some things must *stay out*
slides.picture: An old support ticket carrying a password and personal details, stopped at a gate before the model.

narration: Some text must never go in at all.
Keep out anything you are not allowed to keep.
Also keep out anything you would not want the model to say back.
Old support tickets can hold passwords.
Those stay out.
Personal data stays out if you have no legal reason to keep it.
Private legal advice stays out too.

slides.caption: Keep out anything you may not keep or would not want said back. That includes passwords, personal data and private legal advice.

slides.title: Tables and records stay *out*
slides.text: The model looks them up through a tool instead.
slides.picture: Papers going into a model, while a filing cabinet of records stands apart, joined only by a thin cord.

narration: Some data is not written text at all.
It sits in tables and records.
That data stays out of the corpus too.
When the model needs that data, it looks it up.
It asks a small program to fetch it.
A program like this is called a tool.

slides.caption: Data kept in tables and records stays out of the corpus. The model looks it up through a tool instead.

slides.title: You need the *right* to train
slides.text: Check you are allowed to train on the text.

narration: Next comes the question of rights.
Before training, check that you are allowed to use the text this way.
Being able to read the text does not always mean you may train on it.

slides.caption: Before training, check that you have the right to train on the text.

slides.title: The model *inherits* the rules
slides.text: A model trained on your text is made from that text.
slides.picture: The same tag tied to a stack of papers and to the model trained on them.

narration: Rules also follow the text into the model.
A model trained on your corpus is made from that corpus.
So the rules for that text now apply to the model too.
Some rules say how sensitive the text is.
Some say where it may be kept.
Some say when it must be deleted.
And a model cannot forget just one thing.
If one record must be deleted, the model cannot drop just that record.

slides.caption: Rules about sensitivity, storage and deletion follow the text into the model. A model cannot forget just one record.

slides.title: Mix in *general* text
slides.text: Your text alone can make the model worse at everything else.
slides.picture: Your own papers and everyday papers pouring together into one funnel above a model.

narration: One more thing goes into the corpus.
If you train only on your own text, the model gets better at your field.
But it can get worse at everything else.
It loses some of the general skills it had before.
This is called forgetting.
So your text is mixed with general text.
General text is everyday writing on every kind of subject.
It helps the model keep its general skills.

slides.caption: Training only on your own text can make the model forget general skills. Mixing in general text helps it keep them.

slides.title: One study split a *fixed budget*
slides.text: One study, three fields, one model size.
slides.picture: One tray holding a very tall stack of plain papers and a tiny stack of two cards.

narration: With the corpus ready, the next question is how to share out the training.
Say you can afford a fixed amount of training.
You must decide how much goes to continued pretraining and how much to fine-tuning.
One study tested exactly this.
It looked at health, chemistry and coding.
In each one, the best split put almost everything into continued pretraining.
It is one study at one model size.
Use it as a direction.
Do not copy the exact split.

slides.caption: One study, published on OpenReview on 8 October 2025, split a fixed training budget. Almost all of it went to continued pretraining. It is a single study at one model size.

slides.title: Big job first, *small job* on top

narration: So the lesson is about order and size.
Learning your field is the big job.
It comes first, and it uses raw text.
Learning the task is the small job on top.
It uses question and answer pairs.
Some teams write tens of thousands of pairs by hand to add knowledge.
That is the wrong way to do the big job.

slides.caption: Learning your field is the big job. It uses raw text. Learning the task is the small job on top. It uses pairs.

slides.title: What a general model *misreads*

narration: Now let us see what this changes in practice.
A general model is one trained only on general text.
Here is what it gets wrong in your field.
It reads a common word in its everyday sense.
Your field may use that word to mean something else.
It treats your reference codes as noise.
It takes your insider slang for a typo.

slides.caption: A general model reads common words in their everyday sense. It treats reference codes as noise and insider slang as typos.

slides.title: Explained again on every *request*
slides.text: Continued pretraining puts the knowledge into the model.
slides.picture: A short note on its way to a model, with a thick booklet of explanations clipped to it.

narration: Every one of these misses costs something.
The terms must be looked up and explained on every request.
Looking up text to add to a request is called retrieval.
The system still works.
But everything has to be explained each time.
Continued pretraining puts that knowledge into the model itself.
Then the terms no longer need explaining each time.

slides.caption: Without this training, retrieval must explain the terms on every request. Continued pretraining puts that knowledge into the model itself.

slides.title: The *order* of work

narration: Here is the order of work.
First, continued pretraining on the corpus teaches your field.
If the model was fine-tuned before, run that fine-tuning again on top.
This brings back the style and format of its answers.
Next, test the model's general skills.
If they are damaged, repair them.
Use the fix for forgetting from the distillation chapter.
Your system may send each request to a model of the right size.
This is called routing.
Last, check the routing again.
A small model that knows your field can now take more routine requests.

slides.caption: Train on the corpus. Run fine-tuning again. Test general skills and repair any damage. Last, check the routing again.

slides.title: What changes *afterwards*

narration: So what changes afterwards?
Retrieval stops spending its space on definitions.
It brings back evidence for the task instead.
The text sent to the model with each request is called the prompt.
Prompts get shorter.
A list of definitions no longer needs pasting in.
Each request spends fewer tokens on explaining terms.
So each request costs less.
The model also makes better use of what retrieval finds.

slides.caption: Retrieval brings back evidence instead of definitions. Prompts get shorter. Fewer tokens go on explaining terms. What is retrieved gets used better.

slides.title: The test for *moving on*

narration: So when should you move past this step?
There is rarely anywhere further to go.
Continued pretraining plus fine-tuning is the end of the road for almost every organisation.
The last chapter is custom pretraining and architecture.
It is only for data that is not text at all.

slides.caption: For almost every organisation this is the end of the ladder. Move on only if your data is not text.

slides.title: What to *remember*
items: The text is its own teacher
Preparing the corpus is the project
Rarely any need to go further

narration: Here is what to remember.
A model learns your field by guessing the next word in your own text.
Preparing that text is where the project is won or lost.
Mix in general text to keep the model's general skills.
Learn the field first, from raw text.
Then learn the task on top, from pairs.
For almost everyone, this is as far as the ladder needs to go.
The next and last chapter is custom pretraining and architecture.

slides.caption: A model learns your field from your own text. Preparing that text is the project. Mix in general text, learn the field before the task, and rarely go further.
